articles.title: The empty toolbar icon problem
articles.excerpt: There's a moment every Chrome extension has to survive, and it isn't the Store listing or the marketing site. It's the moment after Chrome says the extension is added. The icon is sitting in the toolb…
articles.body: There's a moment every Chrome extension has to survive, and it isn't the Store listing or the marketing site. It's the moment after Chrome says the extension is added. The icon is sitting in the toolbar and nothing useful has happened yet. That moment is quiet, and it's where a lot of small tools fail. Not because the idea was wrong, but because the first session never gave someone a reason to do the one action that makes the product real. I build PromptAlo, a free Chrome extension for keeping prompts that already worked in chat so you can find them again later. Anything you save goes back into ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini with one click. This piece isn't a walkthrough of buttons. It's a look at the first-run problem for small extensions, with PromptAlo as the example.

articles.body: On a simulator or a phone connected by cable, opening a deep link is one command: # iOS Simulator xcrun simctl openurl booted "myapp://orders/1234" # Android device or emulator over adb adb shell am start -W -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "myapp://orders/1234" On the phone in your hand, with no cable and no terminal, most of us do something worse. We paste the link into Notes, send it to ourselves in Slack, or email it to our own address, then tap it and hope it opens the right screen. When the order number changes, we do it again. It gets harder when someone else reports the bug. The ticket says "open this link on a device and check the order screen", and someone has to get that link onto a phone, open it, and write down what happened.

articles.title: The death of the craft: Why development feels completely empty now.
articles.excerpt: I’ve been a backend dev for about four years, and lately, I feel like I'm attending the funeral of my own profession every single morning at the daily stand-up. I am grieving a job that, technically,…
articles.body: I’ve been a backend dev for about four years, and lately, I feel like I'm attending the funeral of my own profession every single morning at the daily stand-up. I am grieving a job that, technically, still exists. My title hasn't changed, my salary is the same, but the day-to-day reality of what I actually do is completely unrecognizable. We used to be the ones who built things from the ground up. We were engineers. Now, I spend half my day babysitting a machine , acting as a glorified editor for an LLM that hallucinates business logic. When I first started in this industry, the absolute best part of the job was getting stuck . That sounds masochistic, but anyone who actually likes coding knows exactly what I mean. You'd hit a wall with a weird race condition or a database deadlock.

articles.title: ZipMania: A Windows Archive Manager with In-Archive Previews
articles.excerpt: ZipMania is a free, open-source archive manager for Windows 10 and 11. It brings archive browsing, file previews, and Windows Explorer integration together in one desktop app. Browse before extracting…
articles.body: ZipMania is a free, open-source archive manager for Windows 10 and 11. It brings archive browsing, file previews, and Windows Explorer integration together in one desktop app. Browse before extracting ZipMania can preview images and text files inside supported archives, so you can check contents without first unpacking everything. It supports common formats including ZIP, 7Z, RAR, EGG, ALZ, and ISO. A ZIP engine designed for parallel processing When creating ZIP archives, ZipMania can process multiple files in parallel. For large files, it can also divide the data into chunks for parallel deflate. This gives users another way to make use of available CPU resources during compression. Actual results depend on the files, hardware, and settings.

articles.title: 🧩 JavaScript Promises Inside Promises: The Hidden Bugs, Execution Flow and How to Fix Them
articles.excerpt: Have you ever debugged JavaScript code where a function says “Done!”, but the operation it depends on is still running? Or perhaps an API request fails, but the error never reaches the catch() block y…
articles.body: Have you ever debugged JavaScript code where a function says “Done!” , but the operation it depends on is still running? Or perhaps an API request fails, but the error never reaches the catch() block you expected to handle it. You inspect the code. You see .then() , another .then() , maybe a new Promise() inside another Promise and suddenly the execution flow becomes difficult to follow. Sound familiar? As JavaScript developers, we use Promises for API calls, database operations, file processing, authentication, background tasks and countless other asynchronous operations. Yet some of the bugs we encounter aren't caused by Promises themselves. They're caused by how we connect them. Consider this example: fetchUser () . then (( user ) => { saveUser ( user ); }) .

articles.title: How LLMs Work: A Journey Through One Sentence
articles.excerpt: How LLMs Work: A Journey Through Tokens, Attention, and Transformers “My favourite rock band is…” How does a large language model take that unfinished sentence and decide what comes next? You’ve proba…
articles.body: How LLMs Work: A Journey Through Tokens, Attention, and Transformers “My favourite rock band is…” How does a large language model take that unfinished sentence and decide what comes next? You’ve probably heard that LLMs “predict the next token”. But that explanation skips the interesting part: everything that happens between typing a sentence and getting a prediction. So, let’s follow that sentence through a transformer, from text to numbers, through embeddings and attention, all the way to the next token. I made a video walking through this journey, with vectors, matrix shapes, and probably more rock references than strictly necessary. Watch it here, or keep reading for the written walkthrough. We’ll use a simplified GPT-style, decoder-only transformer.

articles.body: Although I count the original Game Boy as one of my first tech obsessions, I still consider Nintendo’s Game Boy Advance to be my favorite console of all time thanks to its more comfortable horizontal design (for my big hands) and its expansive catalog of excellent 32-bit and 16-bit games. Ayaneo isn’t the first company to attempt to modernize the GBA, but its Konkr Pocket Advance does it best. The handheld strikes a near perfect balance between authentically re-creating the GBA’s design while updating its hardware with new controls, a much better screen, and the flexibility of Android at a price that feels like a bargain. articles.title: PS3 games hogging storage on your Android device? This ARMSX3 feature is for you.
articles.excerpt: ARMSX3 now plays CHD files, which delivers much smaller file sizes than conventional ISO files.
articles.body: Credit: Hadlee Simons / Android Authority TL;DR A recent ARMSX3 update has introduced support for playing games in the CHD format. This compressed format can shave gigabytes off your PS3 game files. The update also offers improved frame generation and fewer stutters in certain PS3 games. PlayStation 3 emulation on Android made major strides in recent months thanks to the ARMSX3 app. However, one potential issue is that PS3 games can hog a ton of space on your Android device. Fortunately, a recent ARMSX3 update helps address this issue. The team behind ARMSX3 recently released v1.0.6 of the emulator on GitHub , and it now supports CHD disc images. CHD (Compressed Hunks of Data) is a compression format that delivers smaller file sizes than conventional ISOs.

articles.excerpt: NASA selected 16 companies to provide Enterprise Logistics Support Services under new agreements that will standardize requirements, improve reporting, and streamline the management of costs and resou…
articles.body: Credit: NASA NASA selected 16 companies to provide Enterprise Logistics Support Services under new agreements that will standardize requirements, improve reporting, and streamline the management of costs and resources. The $1.4 billion blanket purchase agreements will support equipment and property management, transportation, disposal, product support, flight hardware support operations, equipment maintenance and repair, export control, move operations, flight hardware, and other material purchases. Under the General Services Administration’s One Acquisition Solution for Integrated Services Plus multiple-award blanket purchase agreements, NASA has the discretion to use firm-fixed-price, time-and-materials, labor-hour, or hybrid contract types.

articles.excerpt: In this Oct. 1, 2026, photo, a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft launch from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The spacecraft is carrying NASA astron…
articles.body: NASA/Joel Kowsky In this Oct. 1, 2026, photo, a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft launch from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The spacecraft is carrying NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov to the International Space Station for a long-duration science mission. They are expected to dock at the space station at 7 p.m. EDT. NASA will stream Crew‑13’s arrival across multiple platforms. The agency’s live broadcast begins at 5:20 p.m. EDT. Learn where to watch at: https://www.nasa.gov/live Learn more about the Crew-13 launch and mission. Image credit: NASA/Joel Kowsky
